intro.text: You own a decrepit narrowboat that will not leave its mooring, because {C02} in the cabin still considers himself its captain. Your sister left you the boat, the cat, and a cabin full of unpaid repair bills. {C01} came with a solicitor's letter, a deadline, and a list of money he expects back. The water against the hull makes no correction.

description.text: Your palms are raw from the mooring line, and the cabin smells of wet wool. Somewhere under the floor, a brass bell has been rung once and not apologized for.
You look like someone who has been forgiven: less paint under your nails, a phone in your pocket with {C01}'s name on it, and a silence in the cabin that is only half your own.
You look borrowed: {C01}'s solicitor's letter in your pocket, a key you do not want to turn, and your sister's cat watching you from the stern as if you are the one about to be sold.
There is a captain's shadow in your posture: you check the water before the tiller, and the cold at your shoulder has a name.
You have stopped answering to the tiller; the boat's cold follows you like a debt, and your hands keep reaching for a rope that isn't there.
You are the person with the keys, the unpaid bills, and a cat that trusts you because you have nowhere else to be; the boat waits to learn your name.

says.text: Since you touched the mooring line, the boat feels less like an estate and more like a mouth: it has swallowed your hands, your deadline, and the name of the man who used to steer it.

Your sister left you the boat the way people leave a mistake: with the keys, the bills, and the cat, as if the debt could be moved into another set of hands. You keep telling yourself you are only selling it.

{C01} stands by the tiller like a man who has decided to trust you, which makes you want to apologize for the boat, the cat, and the dead man all at once. You do not know what you would do with his trust if you had it longer than a day.

{C01} counts the unpaid invoices the way other people count exits. You can hear him deciding whether you are the owner or the obstacle, and the cat has learned to sit between you so neither of you has to say it.
{C01} came with a solicitor's letter and a deadline, which is a polite way of saying he wants his money back before the boat does something unforgivable. You like him. That is the problem.
When you answer to the tiller, {C02} approves of you the way a lighthouse approves of a ship: cold, brief, and from a great distance. You do not know if you have become his first mate or his invoice.

You have stopped saying 'sir' to the cold, and now the cold says it back. {C02} is in the cabin with the look of a man who has been waiting for you to make a mistake, and the tiller is warm only when he is not watching.

{C02} is not a story. {C02} is a set of hands under the floor, a bell that rings when the water rises, and a voice that calls the boat 'mine' in a way that makes your own key feel provisional. You are trying to sell a ship that believes it has a captain.

The buyer's money is real enough to pay {C01}, and that makes it worse: it is a door opening onto a boat without the cat, without {C02}'s cold, without the only person who has ever told you the water's name. You are not sure which of you is being sold.

The deadline is a number in {C01}'s letter, but in the cabin it has become a sound: the mooring line tightening, the cat's bell not ringing, the tiller waiting to see whether you will sign or steer. You need enough left to pay him out and keep the cat. You are not sure what that leaves for you.

The boat moved, and now the question is no longer whether you can sell it but whether you will: the tiller fits your hands like a name, and the dead captain's cold has a place at your shoulder that feels less like fear and more like a berth. You do not know if you are the owner or the first passenger.

The tiller asks a question you did not know you could answer: do you take the boat as property, as crew, or as a sale? Your hands want the rope, your pocket wants the letter, and the water wants a name. You have not chosen.

The mooring line is not just rope; it is a sentence the boat says to the water. When you held it, you felt the dead captain's grip under yours, and now you cannot tell whether you learned its name or it learned yours.

emerson_trust.meaning: How far Emerson believes you will deliver the sale and his money before the deadline without letting the ghost stop the business.

hugh_obedience.meaning: How far you answer Hugh as captain rather than owner, using his terms, his corrections, and his authority over the boat.

description.text: The stern deck is an open rectangle of wet planking. The cabin door is on one side, the low rail around the edge, and a hatch opens over the tiller well. The sky keeps the deck grey. The air smells of tar, wet canvas, and cold iron. A brass plaque by the cabin door gives the boat's name in letters worn smooth by a thumb that is no longer here.

exits.label: down the hatch to the companionway

description.text: The tiller well is a narrow pit in the stern deck, where the tiller rises from the hull. Its brass grip is dark with old hand sweat and newer rain. Chains run down out of sight, and the well smells of oil and wet rope. A small oilcan sits in a cradle on the bulkhead. The cabin hatch overhead lets the weather in.

The mooring platform is a narrow ledge of boards at the very stern, with a bollard, a cleat, and a ring for a line where the boat meets the canal. The boards are slick with algae and rain. The water laps close enough to hear the hull settle. A rusted hook hangs from the rail, and the edge is worn down where someone has stood a long time.

The cabin is a low, narrow room under the boat's roof, with a bench along one side and a small table under a hanging lamp. The stove is blackened and the porthole is fogged, so the light comes in as a grey smear. The air smells of damp wool, cold tea, and the tar smell of the hull. A curtain at the door has been stitched over a hole and hangs straight.

A short slab of damp concrete runs from the hull to the water's edge, slick under your boots. A green bollard and an iron ring are set into its corner, and a drain line cuts the concrete near the toe. Water against the hull and wind in the rigging are the only sounds. It smells of wet stone, rope tar, and cold canal water. The bollard's paint is scaled where lines have been hauled across it for years.

The lock mouth is a narrow throat of stone and iron where the canal water meets the slip. A pitted gate face stands at the water's edge, and a rusted ladder climbs from the sill to the concrete above. The air is colder here. It smells of green water, wet iron, and the oil from the lock's old chains.

The bow is a narrow deck of grey planks, ending at a low iron rail. A brass nameplate hangs above the bow, and a compass is bracketed to the stem. The light comes off the water and makes the paint look like wet slate. You smell cold iron, paraffin, and canal weed under the hull.

The deck narrows back toward the cabin door. A pale stripe is worn through the paint where feet and paws have passed. A small hatch plate is riveted in the centre, and the planks rise and fall with the water. You smell wet hemp and old oil. The light is a flat grey, and every crack looks like a mouth that has been told to keep quiet.

You are in a low brick hut at the lock's edge, half office, half machine shed. A desk under the window faces the water and the mooring. The air tastes of wet wool and paraffin. The single bulb throws a yellow pool over the instruments. {C03}'s coat hangs by the wall, and chain passes through a slot in the floor.

A narrow hatch in the stern deck drops into a short stair that smells of wet wool and old varnish. The handrail is painted black and cold enough to sting the palm. At the bottom, the cabin door stands open just far enough to admit a draught. The draught smells faintly of pipe tobacco that has not been lit for thirty years.

The rusted iron ladder hangs from the mooring platform, its lower rungs just kissing the black water. One side is bent outward in a gentle arc, as if it has been leaning on something that leaned back. The rope cowl at the top is frayed. The ladder creaks in time with the boat's own slow breathing. The water under the lowest rung is black.

The bow deck opens through a low hatch into the cabin, the glass panel clouded with condensation and a single smudge where a thumb has wiped it clean. The step is worn into a shallow bowl, and the hinge pin is packed with a stiff, grey grit. When it opens, the cabin exhales a breath held too long, and the cold follows the hinge into the deck.

A narrow concrete path runs along the lock wall, cracked, furred with moss, and holding one puddle that has never quite dried. The lock wheel looms above it, its rusted spokes making a face if you are not expecting one. At the far end, the lock-keeper's hut door is propped open with a brick. The brick is colder than it should be.

The cabin door is small, with a brass latch shaped like a wheel. The paint is blistered where rain has worked at it for years. The seam is dark with mildew, and the handle is cold even when the air is not.

The stern rail is low iron around the deck's edge, painted the colour of dried blood and worn bright where hands have gripped it in weather. One upright is bent slightly outward, as if it has taken a blow and decided to keep going.

{C01}'s phone is cracked in a case with a canal map sticker, its screen fogged with rain and impatience. The battery icon is always low enough to make {C01} hold it up to the sky for signal, as if the signal were a person who could be shouted at.
Your phone is damp where the rain has found the screen, and the case has a chip along one corner. The lock-keeper's number is saved under a name you did not choose.

A folded sheaf of papers with {C03}'s handwriting on the top page, the edges soft and grey where they have been carried in a pocket. The sale terms are printed in small type, and the deadline is underlined twice.

A ring of keys on a red cord, one of them shaped like a little boat and another that has worn its teeth smooth. The ring clinks against the deck when it is moved, and the cord has a knot in it that was never meant to be there.

A broad tiller of varnished wood rising from the hull, its brass grip dark with old hand sweat and newer rain. The wood is scarred where it has been pulled hard, and the grain runs in a line that looks like a river seen from above.
Chains run down from the tiller into the hull, their links black with scale and wet. They move when the boat settles, and the sound they make is not quite the sound of chains.

The tiller's brass grip is worn to a hollow where a palm would rest, the metal cold and faintly green at the edges. There is a small dent in one side, as if someone's ring has been pressed there many times.

A water-stained log in a cracked leather cover, its pages swollen with old rain and newer salt. The last entry is in a hand that is careful and very old, and the final line has been crossed out so hard the pen has torn the paper.
A dented oilcan with a spout that drips when it is tilted, the label peeling in long grey strips. It smells of oil and something underneath it, like a cold room that has been shut for a long time.

A thick mooring line coiled around the bollard, its fibres dark with water and old tar. The rope is worn smooth where it has been handled, and the end is knotted in a way that looks deliberate, as if it were tightening into a knot you did not tie.
A thinner line than the mooring line, with a red tag tied to it that has faded to the colour of old paper. It is coiled loosely on the platform, and the tag has been written on more than once.

A short iron bollard set into the platform, its top worn to a dull shine and its base ringed with rust. The metal is cold to the touch, and the bollard's shadow falls straight down even when the light is not.
A small brass cleat bolted to the platform, its horns rounded with years of rope and weather. One bolt is loose, and the cleat creaks when the boat settles.

A rusted hook hanging from the rail, its curve worn smooth where it has been used to pull a line aboard. The hook is cold, and the ring it hangs from has been turned so many times that the metal is bright.
A spare line coiled at the platform's edge, its end knotted to a ring in the rail. The rope is older than the others, and the knot has been dressed so carefully that it looks carved rather than tied.
A long seat with a canvas cover, worn smooth where someone sat for years. A brass button from a uniform is sewn into the canvas, and the middle of the seat is thinner than the rest.
A small folding table with a warped top and a drawer that sticks. A ring from a cup has marked the wood, and a corner is worn down where papers have been laid out.
A bread knife with a cracked handle and a blade that has been sharpened too often. It is the only sharp thing in the cabin, and it has been used for more than bread.
A dented tin cup with a chip in the rim, the kind that keeps tea hot too long. It has a faint blue line around the lip, as if it was made for someone who liked to keep score.
A patch of air by the bench makes the hair on your arms stand up. It does not move like weather; it waits.
A cream envelope, addressed in a hand that has crossed out the name twice. The date is the day after the deadline, and the corner is bent from being held too long.
A brass lamp with a cracked glass chimney, swinging when the boat is decided against. The bulb is old and has a dark ring inside where the wick used to be.
A small stove with a blackened door and a handle wrapped in wire. It has not been lit in years, but the ash inside is still cold.
A green-painted bollard with a flat top and a scar of old rope around its throat. Under the cap, a faint H has been scratched into the paint, too deliberate to be an accident.
A neat bowline sits at the bollard's throat, tied in your own hand. The rope is pale where it has been pulled taut, and the knot has not slipped. It has been pulled once, hard.
A cut end of mooring rope lies coiled at your feet. The fibres are frayed and damp. It still smells faintly of the cabin knife's oil.
A slate board hangs on a bent bracket, chalked with old marks and a small square where {C03} counts boats. The lowest mark has been rubbed over so many times the slate is shiny.
A shallow channel is cut into the concrete, running to the water's edge. It is stained black with old rope fibre and a little green algae.
A pitted iron gate face, green with water and rust, is set into the lock's stone sill. A small brass ring is fixed to its lower corner. It is worn smooth by a thumb that is no longer here.
A steel gauge is bolted to the stone, its scale marked in inches. A small arrow is bent by a hand that wanted the water higher. It points just above the line where the hull sits.
A short iron ladder climbs from the sill to the concrete above. One rung is bent where a boot has kicked it too many times. The rungs are slick with green water.
A heavy chain hangs from a hook in the stone, its links thick with rust and a thin coat of oil. One link is slightly open. It has been pulled and not quite closed.
A wide slab of wet stone runs along the lock mouth. Its edge is worn to a soft curve where boats have been nudged past. A dark stain on the sill matches the hull's waterline exactly.

A wicker basket holds a blue blanket folded inside. One corner is chewed into a neat square. A small brass bell is tied to the rim with string. The string has been replaced twice, and the bell has not been moved from the rim.

The low iron rail has paint bubbling at the joints. A dent on one bar is shaped like a closed fist. The metal is worn smooth where hands have gripped it, and the wear is square, as if the hand had been checking the rail for something.

A brass plate has a name in curved letters. The name has been scratched through once, then scratched over again in a different hand. The final letter has been filed down so hard it is almost gone, and the brass beneath is worn smooth by a thumb that is no longer here.
A round compass sits in a brass bracket, its glass clouded with age. The needle points steadily toward the lock. It has the patience of an instrument that has never heard of anywhere else.
A small oil lamp is caged in wire. The glass is cracked, but the crack is sealed with a ring of old putty. The wick is black. One bar of the cage holds a hair, and the hair has not been combed out.

A long pale line runs through the paint, raised like a ridge under the surface. It goes from the waterline up to the rail. It has been painted over so many times it has become its own colour, and the colour has stopped answering to the rest of the hull.

A coil of hemp lies on the deck. The knot has been pulled apart and re-tied so often the fibres stand out like bristles. One end is stained dark. The tag is missing, and the rope has kept the shape of a tag that is no longer there.

A square of green oilskin is nailed down at the corners. The middle is worn to a pale stripe where {C04} has waited. A paw print is pressed into the dust in the centre, and the nails are rusted through.

A small rectangular hatch plate is riveted into the deck. The hasp is bent back and forth until it is almost split. The plate is warm to the touch even when the air is cold, and the warmth has the regularity of something that has been closed and opened on purpose.

A riveted metal plate has a number stamped into it. The digits are filled with black paint, then scratched out again. The rivets are green with old water. One has been hit by a hammer, and the dent is in the shape of a correction.

A brass strainer is set into the deck. The mesh is clogged with weed and a single button. The button is small, black, and has no jacket to match it. It has been washed down here, and the water has not returned it.

A single board rocks when stepped on. The nails are pulled short, and the wood is grey with weather. It has been painted the same colour as the rest of the deck, but it still creaks a note lower than the others, as if it has been told to sit down.

A dark patch on the deck is shaped like a hand, the fingers spread and the thumb bent. It has been there long enough to be part of the wood. It does not dry when the rest of the deck does, and the stain keeps its shape the way a knot keeps a rope.
The scarred pine desk has a drawer that sticks, a blotter stained like a tide chart, and a pencil groove worn into the edge where a hundred lock ledgers sat.
A solicitor's card is taped to the desk. The date is crossed out and rewritten in red. The bottom edge is damp, as if held by wet hands.
The solid door has a brass handle and a keyhole worn square. The rubber flap at the bottom has torn, leaving a permanent gap that lets in the lock's damp.
The black telephone sits on the desk, its handset resting on the cradle. The cord is coiled like a sleeping snake. The dial tone has been dead since the last owner left.
The black kettle has a dent in the lid and a handle wrapped in wire. The water inside has been boiled so often it tastes of metal.
The water-warped ledger lists boats through the lock. The last entry is in {C03}'s careful hand: 'the boat – will not move.'
The chair has a missing leg propped on a brick. The seat is worn to a hollow where {C03} waits.
The single pane has a latch that only works by rattle. The glass is fogged where someone has breathed on it. Outside, the water is black.
The hatch is latched with a brass hook, worn smooth by a thumb that is no longer here, then filed down to a nub. The latch will not stay down for more than a few seconds.
The paint is cracked into little islands of black, and one rung is wrapped in a strip of tape labelled C.H. in pencil.
It is green with algae and slick under your fingers. There is a single boot print in the slime, too small to be anyone's on the boat.
The smudge is in the shape of a thumb, but the print is too large for either of you. It is still faintly oily, and the glass around it is clouded.
The grit is canal silt, mixed with something finer, like ash from a very old match. It sits in the hinge pin and does not shift.
One spoke is bent inward. The bend is fresh enough to still smell of hot iron, and the wheel does not turn when you push it.
It is a standard red brick. The mortar between the bricks is the wrong colour, a pale blue that matches the water in the lock.
A brass cabin key on a loop of your sister's twine. It fits the lock, but sometimes the lock seems to fit you first.
A solicitor's letter in {C01}'s hand, the deadline underlined twice; you have folded it into a small, papery coin in your pocket.
A grey rag, damp at one corner, folded the way someone who expects to be interrupted folds things.
A short pencil, chewed at one end, lying in the rain near the cabin door. It is enough to write a date on a wrist.
A short coil of spare line, dry and stiff, with a frayed end that has never been tied.
A cheap pen, capped, lying beside the sale papers as if it had been waiting for a signature.
{C03}'s buyer papers are open and waiting, the pen cap still on the paper.
A pen with a cap that has been off recently, though the ink is still dark.

C01.name: Emerson Whitlock

description.text: {C01} stands with the phone open to the solicitor, not hiding it. When he catches you looking, he taps the date: there, the number, the name.
{C01} keeps the cash in one fist and the letter in the other. He checks his watch like the boat is a line item he can write off.
{C01} watches the tiller for a second, then checks the letter again, as if the boat has just agreed to something.
{C01} keeps his hand on the letter. His eyes flick to the tiller, as if the boat is a debt that might jump.
{C01}'s thumb hovers over the solicitor's number. It does not press, as if the letter in your hand has made the call less certain.
{C01} is the wet-jacketed brother-in-law, phone in one hand, a solicitor's letter in the other, checking the time like it owes him money.

here.text: {C01} holds the phone up to the sky for signal, the solicitor's letter loose in the other hand.
{C01} counts cash into a pocket, one eye on the mooring line.
{C01} checks the mooring line, then the letter, as if the boat has just answered a question.
{C01} watches the tiller, phone raised, as if the boat is about to cost him something.
{C01} holds the letter by the corner, thumb over the solicitor's number but not calling.
{C01} is in a wet jacket, phone raised for signal, a solicitor's letter in the other hand.

says.text: 'The deadline's in the letter. The solicitor's not negotiating with weather.' He taps the date written on his wrist once. 'Give me a time, not a mood.'
'I paid for repairs, not a séance.' He checks the date on his wrist. 'If the papers aren't done by that, I'm calling the solicitor and the boat's a problem.'
'It's a date, not a threat. The solicitor doesn't care about the tiller, he cares about the date.'
'The money's here. Count it if you like.' He holds the cash out, then pulls it back. 'Sign, and it's settled.'
'I fronted the cash when the boat was still a liability.' He checks his phone. 'If you make me wait for a ghost, I'm taking it back with interest.'
'It's not charity. It's repairs, paid, with a deadline attached.'
'Read it. Date, name, amount.' He holds the letter out. 'No room for a cold spot.'
'I'm not hiding it, I'm holding it.' He checks the rain. 'If you want the sale, let the paper do the talking.'
He doesn't take the letter back. 'If it's going to be filed, let it be filed properly.'
'It's not a letter, it's a deadline. The solicitor's voice on the phone is the same as the ink.'
'{C03}'s the buyer. The papers say so.' He checks the rain. 'If they're coming, I want the money before the boat moves.'
'A buyer doesn't care about a cat or a cold cabin.' He taps the letter. 'If the buyer isn't coming, tell me what is.'
'Is the buyer coming, or is the boat going elsewhere? Pick one before I pick a problem.'
'The letter names a buyer. That's all I need to know, unless the buyer's a rumor.'
'A cat's a liability, not a feature.' He checks the phone. 'It sells as sold, not as a cautionary tale.'
'How does a cat boat sell? That's the question.' He waits for the rain to answer. 'If you prioritize the cat, I prioritize the money.'
'The buyer will see a cat. I'll see a discount.'
'Name it right and it holds. That's the whole job.' He points at the line. 'Don't make me listen to a ghost for a knot.'
'You called it wrong and now it's knotted.' He checks the bollard. 'A line isn't a conversation, it's a cost.'
'If it's named right, it holds. I don't care if the boat's cold.' He checks the line. 'That's the sale.'
'It's knotted like it's got a grudge.' He checks the phone. 'I paid for repairs, not a temper.'
'It's a mooring line. Say it like you mean to keep the boat where it is.'
'Sign over the proceeds and we're done.' He checks the cash. 'I don't want your feelings, I want the number.'
'If the ghost stops the sale, I'm taking your share too.' He checks the phone. 'That's what a deadline means.'
'The boat's money is my money until it's paid. Sign when the ink is dry.'
'{C02} is negotiable. If the date is real, the captain can keep the wheel and I can keep the money.'
'{C02} is not a haunting, he is a lien. If he keeps the boat, he keeps my work money.'
'If the captain keeps the wheel, we are one step ahead. If he does not, we are still in the cold.'
"{C02} is not keeping the wheel, and the boat is already charging us for the delay."
"{C02} is a defect with a voice. Get the date signed, and {C02} can keep the tiller."
"{C03} says yes or no to the water. Keep {C03} on the phone; every delay is a lost day."
"{C04} is a marketing asset. List it as a feature, and the buyer will want it."
"{C04} is a liability. Keep {C04} off the line, or the sale will not move."
"{C04} is a liability. The knot under {C04} is a deduction from the sale."
"The stern deck is the only place with enough sky for a signal and enough rain to make the delay worth paying for."
"The cabin smells like tea and old decisions. Do not let {C02} set the terms in there."
"The boat is not sold, so it is not ours. It is not ours, so it is not our problem. The line is still our problem."
"Do not stand there. The bow is for looking at the sale, not the fog."
"That is where the water says yes or no. Stay there, or we are not in control."
"No signal means no proof, but the date is still proof. Get the letter, and the money will follow."
"No signal means no proof. {C02} is the only witness, and witnesses do not pay."
"One bar is a delay, not a fate. The date is real, and the sky will answer."
"A letter in a cold room is still a letter. Sign it, date it, and the cabin becomes a room again."
"A letter in a cold room is a trap. It is not signed, so it is just weather."
"The letter does not care about the tea. Date it, and it is done."
"It is not a phone. It is the only witness that pays me back."
"Answer when it rings. The silence is the network trying to sell us too."
"The papers are a promise. The sale is clean, and the papers are clean."
"The papers are leverage. Hold them until the money clears, or they are just paper."
"The papers are the only thing that can outrun the fog. Sign, date, done."
"The tiller is the sale. When it moves, we move."
"Cold is a defect. List it, note it, and do not stand in it."
"Keys are a receipt. I have them, and I am not stuck here."
"Keys are a receipt. I have them, and the money is not paid, so I am not coming back."
"Keys are leverage. Money is the point."
"Tighten it. A loose line is a loose sale."
"Bollards hold lines. Lines hold boats. Boats hold dates."
"Sit down if you want. The date will not."
"The table is for the letter, not the tea."
"The knife is for the envelope, not {C02}."
"The cup is a decoration. It steams, and it is a defect."

C01.history: Emerson paid for the boat's repairs before the legal deadline, expecting the sale to settle the debt. He came to help you sell it, not to inherit its mood, and he keeps the solicitor's letter and the cash within reach. He loves his sister enough to handle the estate, but he checks the date more often than he checks the water.

C02.name: Hugh Calloway

description.text: {C02}'s hand lies flat on the tiller instead of gripping it, and the chill at {C02}'s shoulder has eased to a clean ship's-board cold. When you use the right name, {C02}'s fingers move as if the rope were answering your voice.

{C02} stands square at the tiller, collar straight, and the nearest line tightens against the bollard as you pass. The air around {C02} freezes in small circles, and the hull creaks like a man holding his breath.
{C02}'s tea still steams on the table, and {C02}'s hand has not left the tiller. {C02} looks at the letter, then at you, with the patience of a man who has already decided the terms.
Old naval coat, brass button missing, a face with no more color than wet canvas. {C02} keeps the cap square and the eyes on the wheel as if the canal had not learned to be a canal.

here.text: {C02} has both fists on the tiller, the cap straight, and the cold around {C02} makes the nearest rope hum.
{C02} has one hand loose on the tiller and the other resting near the steaming cup, as if waiting to be corrected.
{C02} has the coat buttoned like a uniform and the eyes on the mooring line as if it had spoken out of turn.

says.text: 'Captain. You have said it without flinching. Now keep the name steady, and the wheel will not bite.'
'You stand in my cabin and call yourself captain. The hull is already writing its complaint.'
'Captain. Not owner, not seller, not man with a deadline. Say it correctly and the boat will not argue.'
'Mooring line. There. You have named it. Now keep the name steady, and the boat will not knot itself in protest.'
'You call it a stern line, and the stern line answers back. That is why it knots.'
'Mooring line, not stern line. And hold your tongue, the wind is not your friend.'
'Sell it if you must. Name the line first, and let the buyer meet the water before the ink dries.'
'You mean to sell my ship while I am still at the wheel? Then let the hull creak for every pound you count.'
'The sale is a paper, and paper does not hold a boat. The line holds the boat.'
'Your sister knew the difference between a lock and the sea. She kept my tea warm and my corrections in her pocket.'
'You have forgotten her first order: a boat is not a thing you move. It is a thing you answer.'
'Your sister moored this boat with respect. That is how a captain is kept, and that is how a line is kept.'
'The cat sits where the line is true. That is more than you have done so far.'
'It will sit on my tiller if you let it, and then you will have a cat for a captain.'
'The cat is not a passenger. It is a witness. It sits where the line is true.'
'{C03} is a buyer, and a buyer is a tide. Let the buyer step aboard; if the line holds, the sale may hold too.'
'You would give my wheel to a name in a letter? The letter will not steer.'
'{C03} is a buyer, and a buyer is a tide. Tides come, tides go, and the boat must still know its line.'

interactions.text: The boat slides clear of the lock, and the water {C02} names opens ahead of her. The slip falls away behind you, and the boat is no longer where it was tied.
You draw oil over the rudder chains, and the squeak goes quiet. The tiller turns with a small, obedient click, as if the boat has been waiting for maintenance.
'Higher than it should be,' {C03} says, and does not look away from the lock gate. 'I'd rather not be right about this one.'
The keys are cold and have no business on a boat that will not move. The ring rattles once in your hand, and then goes still.
{C04} looks at you, then at {C02}, and decides you are both furniture. It blinks once, very slowly, and goes back to pretending it is not in charge of the situation.

events.text: At the mooring point, the lines snap, the boat slides off the lock, {C02}'s hand is on the tiller, {C01}'s hand is on your shoulder, and the water begins to strike the hull.
{C04} walks the deck to {C02} without hurry, as if this is the most reasonable route on the boat.

nudges.text: The mooring line pulls tight with a sound like a bone.
{C01}'s voice carries across the water: 'I'm not getting on this thing until someone tells me what we're doing.'

recap.text: At the mooring point the lines snapped, the boat slid off the lock, {C02}'s hand closed on the tiller, and {C01}'s gripped your shoulder as water struck the hull. {C04} walked the deck to him, {C03} watched, {C01} asked into the phone whether the buyer returned, the mooring line was named correctly, and the unpaid, unsold boat went to the water {C02} named.

E_N05.title: The Lock Is Closed, the Boat Is Going

text.text: The boat leaves the mooring under {C02}'s hand on the tiller and {C03}'s papers in your pocket, with the cat already in the bow and {C01} paid enough to stop pulling you toward the lock. The sale goes through, but the boat moves only because the dead captain was answered, not removed.

variants.text: {C01} takes the keys and the money, leaves before the boat reaches the lock, and becomes a paid creditor who will not hear from you again unless the solicitor calls.
{C01} pockets your share and walks off with the keys, telling the solicitor the boat was sold as seen, leaving you to explain the cat and the cold cabin to a stranger.
variants.note: fallback: the last variant holds otherwise

variants.text: {C02} stays at the tiller as the boat is sold and moving, answering the mooring line you named and letting you remain owner under his wheel.
{C02} stays at the tiller but makes the cabin cold and the hull creak, so the boat moves as a sold vessel with a captain who has not forgiven the name.
variants.note: fallback: the last variant holds otherwise

text.text: The boat is sold to {C03} under your signature and moves under your own hand on the tiller, with the cat in the bow and the lock-keeper coiling the line at the lock. {C01} is paid, takes the keys, and leaves with the money, but the cabin is empty of {C02}'s cup and the cold spot is gone, and the boat answers to the papers alone.

variants.text: {C01} is paid out at the hut and steps back as the boat drifts off, leaving you with the signed papers and the empty cabin.
{C01} takes the buyer's money and your share before the boat moves, and the sale is clean only because he has already decided you were not part of it.
variants.note: fallback: the last variant holds otherwise

variants.text: {C02} lets the cat on the tiller replace him and leaves the cabin empty, so the boat moves under your signature alone.
{C02} is displaced by the cat and the signature, and the cabin empties of him so completely the sale feels like a small death.
variants.note: fallback: the last variant holds otherwise

text.text: The boat leaves the mooring under {C02}'s hand on the tiller and goes to the water he names, with the cat walking the length of the deck and {C03} watching from the bank. {C01} is not paid and does not board; the sale is not made, and the boat is no longer for sale but under the dead captain's orders.

variants.text: {C01} stays steady enough to let you hold the boat, but the unsold papers remain in his hand and he goes with them, unpaid and out of the question.
{C01} grips your shoulder until the water slaps the hull, asks into the phone whether the buyer returns, and leaves the papers in his hand, having lost the deadline and the money.

variants.text: {C02} takes your hand on the tiller and names the water, steering the unsold boat under his terms with you aboard.
{C02} closes his hand on the tiller and names the water before you can answer, taking the course whether you obey or not.
